mcqs.question: For a `withdraw(amount)` method, which statement correctly labels a precondition versus a postcondition?
options: "amount must be positive" is a postcondition; "balance decreases by amount" is a precondition
Both statements are invariants, since they both relate to the same method
Neither statement is part of a contract unless it's enforced with a runtime check
"amount must be positive" is a precondition (the caller's obligation before calling); "balance decreases by exactly amount" is a postcondition (the method's guarantee after it runs)
mcqs.explanation: Preconditions are obligations the caller must satisfy before the call; postconditions are guarantees the method makes after it runs, assuming the precondition held. Swapping the two mislabels which side owns which obligation. Invariants are object-wide rules across all methods, not this pair, and a contract exists conceptually whether or not it's enforced — enforcement is a separate, later design decision.

mcqs.question: In the `Stack.pop()` example, what does adding the explicit `if (items.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalStateException(...)` check actually change about the stack's behavior on an empty stack?
options: It prevents pop() from ever being called on an empty stack
It makes pop() succeed on an empty stack by returning null instead of failing
It changes pop()'s time complexity from O(1) to O(n)
The stack still fails on an empty pop() either way — the check just replaces a confusing generic exception with a clear statement of exactly which contract was violated
mcqs.explanation: An empty stack was always going to fail either way; the precondition check doesn't change whether it fails, only how clearly it communicates why. It doesn't prevent the call from happening, doesn't make it silently succeed with null, and has no effect on time complexity.

mcqs.question: A `BankAccount` class has the invariant "balance is never negative." A new `chargeFee()` method is added later. What does the invariant require of this new method?
options: chargeFee() must independently preserve the invariant — leaving balance never negative after it runs — even though the invariant wasn't declared at that call site
chargeFee() is exempt from the invariant since it was added after the invariant was defined
The invariant only applies to deposit() and withdraw() by name
chargeFee() only needs to satisfy the invariant if it's called directly by external code
mcqs.explanation: A class invariant applies to every public method on the object, including ones written after the invariant was first established — it isn't scoped to the methods that existed when it was defined, isn't named-method-specific, and doesn't distinguish between internal and external callers.

mcqs.question: A method's doc comment says "amount must be positive," but the method has no runtime check and accepts any input silently. What's the risk being described?
options: There is no risk, since the documentation clearly states the requirement
The precondition will rot: new team members, autocomplete, or copy-pasted call sites won't see the comment, and negative amounts will silently corrupt state
Java automatically enforces doc-comment preconditions at compile time
The risk only exists if the method is public and never if it's private
mcqs.explanation: A documented-but-unchecked precondition has no enforcement mechanism, so it silently rots as the code and its readers change over time — the exact failure mode this pitfall describes. Java doesn't enforce doc-comment contracts automatically, and an unchecked precondition risk applies to private methods too, just with a smaller blast radius.
